Business.title: Trump made over 1,000 July stock trades worth up to $270m, filings reveal
Business.text:
Donald Trump made over a thousand stock sales and purchases worth between $79m and $270m in July, according to a Guardian analysis of his latest financial disclosure released Tuesday.

His two largest sales were of Amazon and Microsoft stock, selling between $5m and $25m each on 20 July. That same day, he also sold up to $5m worth of Oracle and Costco stock, $500,000 to $1m in Nvidia, and bought up to $5m worth of shares in Intuit and Salesforce, among dozens of other transactions.

Overall, he made more than 700 sales that totaled between $35m and $137m, and made more than 440 purchases that totaled between $43.5m and $134m. Financial disclosures, which presidents and vice-presidents are required to file by law, only include a date and a range of the transaction amount.

The White House said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio was “independently managed by third-party financial institutions” and that there were no conflicts of interests in the latest disclosure.

“All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson.

“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers.”

The July disclosure comes as Trump and the Republican party continues to champion a ban on stock trading among members of Congress, which would exclude him from any restrictions. The president made more trades than all of Congress combined between the start of his second term and June, a Bloomberg analysis found.

Trump’s last annual financial disclosures revealed that he made more than $2.2bn last year from his network of businesses and investments, including $1bn in crypto revenue. Disclosures from his staff have also revealed large $45,000 cash gifts to three White House officials, including his close personal aide, Natalie Harp, which sparked calls from watchdog groups for further investigation.

Trump also made up to $15.5m from his investments into oil and gas companies, the Senate’s joint economic committee found, because of gas prices driven up by the US war with Iran.

The president, vice-president and members of Congress are legally allowed to trade stocks and are required to disclose their trades within 45 days of the transaction.

But the practice is widely unpopular with voters. A recent survey from the Economist and YouGov found that about 75% of respondents, which included majorities of Democrats and Republicans, believed that elected officials should not be allowed to buy and sell individual stocks in public office.

The Trump-endorsed Stop Insider Trading Act passed by the House of Representatives in July, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The ban, however, would not affect Trump or JD Vance.

Business.title: Patrick Clancy interview on 60 Minutes fails to provide big ratings boost for CBS
Business.text:
60 Minutes’ blockbuster interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, failed to provide a major ratings boost for the Sunday show, according to audience figures released Tuesday.

Sunday night’s episode of the newsmagazine show drew an average of 6.77m total viewers, the third-smallest audience in the past 25 years for the second episode of a season, adding to a disappointing debut for Bari Weiss, who, as CBS editor-in-chief, rewired the show, firing several high-profile correspondents in the run-up to the new season.

The 59th season debuted on 13 September with an audience down sharply from the 58th season debut, drawing 7.94 million viewers compared with 10 million for last season’s first episode.

That episode was the show’s lowest-rated season debut in the 21st century, though CBS News touted it as the most-watched non-sports program of the week and released a statement expressing satisfaction with the content of the program. “We are so proud of the exceptional journalism on display in our season premiere and we can’t wait to bring our audience another amazing show this coming Sunday,” the network said last week.

The 20 September episode of the show barely edged last season’s second episode (6.45 million viewers), and it was likely hurt by not having NFL football as a lead-in program in all markets. But it featured what should have been an audience-boosting interview, with new correspondent Ross Douthat sitting down with Patrick Clancy, who described the killings of his children and the aftermath. Clancy’s new wife, fertility doctor Rachel Danis, also gave a brief interview.

In a nod to the interview’s cultural significance and importance for the show, Weiss was in attendance for the conversation, sources said. The show also featured a timely segment on pushback against datacenters reported by correspondent Norah O’Donnell, along with a whodunnit piece from longtime sports-focused correspondent Jon Wertheim about Shergar, an Irish racehorse kidnapped in the 1980s.

While Douthat’s interview with Clancy received generally favorable reviews, it evidently was not the ratings draw that CBS News executives had hoped. The show’s debut episode had also featured a blockbuster interview, with one of the American fighter pilots shot down over Iran in April.

The Guardian has reached out to CBS News about Sunday’s ratings.

On a positive note for the network, the episode attracted 179.2m social views, surpassing last week’s record of 116.7m views.

Sports.title: England players carrying 'scar' from World Cup exit, says Bukayo Saka
Sports.text:
England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.

Thomas Tuchel's team were on the verge of becoming the first England side to reach a men's World Cup final since 1966, but were stunned by two late Argentina goals as they fell to a 2-1 loss.

A thrilling 6-4 victory over France in the bronze medal match gave the Three Lions their best World Cup finish in six decades, but the wait for their second trophy goes on.

"Obviously, there is still a scar on us when you believed and everyone was so united and so confident we could do it," Saka said.

"Not just us, but the whole country we felt.

"You try to move on as soon as possible, but you know a scar is a scar, it decides to heal when it heals itself."

England get an immediate reminder of what might have been as they host world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday (19:45 BST) in the first of four Nations League matches over the next two weeks.

"We are trying to draw a line under [the World Cup] now and focus on the new international season that we have coming up," Saka added.

"We have got four massive, difficult group games to try and qualify us for the Nations League [knockouts] that we are really focused on."

Meanwhile, Saka believes it is only a matter of time before his Arsenal team-mate Max Dowman, 16, earns a senior England call-up.

"I think so," Saka said. "His talent is insane. It's up to him how far he is going to go in football. His talent is crazy."

England Under-21 manager Lee Carsley concurred with Saka on Dowman's "amazing talent" but thinks the youngster staying with the under-19s during this international window is the best option.

"He is more than capable of playing in the under-21s," Carsley said.

"What I do think will happen with the age group he goes to is that he can play the minutes.

"He can also have that time to consolidate where he is in his career and play with his friends again and take that little bit of pressure off him.

"I have no doubt that Max is going to be with the under-21s.

"That is something I am keen to have a conversation with him and his parents, on the way we see his pathway going, because he is an amazing talent and someone we are very lucky to have."

Sports.title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt, with interest costs rising and £63.5m spent on new stadium
Sports.text:
Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for their new stadium.

Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, United have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.

This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24.

However, while they have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased.

Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, this sum alone has now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005.

In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125 (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club has not explained what it has done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.

It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximated 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.

This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first team squad this summer.

United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans - this summer. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than newly promoted Ipswich.

However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches due to injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.

While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts.

"We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada.

"This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

"While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.

"With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."

United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, which is currently second bottom of the table with one point from three games.

Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m.

"This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

Sports.title: Kimi Antonelli interview: Mercedes driver on moment he knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
Sports.text:
Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.

The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.

A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.

"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."

Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.

"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."

Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.

After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.

Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.

Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.

The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.

He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.

Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.

"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.

"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.

"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.

"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."

Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.

At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.

He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.

Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.

"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.

"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.

"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'

"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."

Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.

"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.

"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.

"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.

"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."

Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.

"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.

"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."

Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.

Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.

All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?

"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.

"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."

His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".

"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.

"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."

There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.

"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.

"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.

"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."

The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.

Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"

He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.

Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.

"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."

All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.

Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.

"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.

"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

Sports.title: Football scouting: Hidden gems and the race to discover emerging talent
Sports.text:
The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.

"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.

Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.

It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.

Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.

"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.

"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."

From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.

"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare."

"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.

Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.

It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.

Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.

The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.

"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."

Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.

The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.

"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."

Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.

"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.

"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."

"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.

"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.

"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."

One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".

Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.

For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.

Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.

As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.

Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.

"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."

Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.

"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.

"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."

One of those markets continues to be Africa.

"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.

Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.

"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.

With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.

But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.

"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.

"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."

Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.

Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.

"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.

"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."

Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.

Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.

"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."

Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.

The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.

It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.

Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.

Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.

Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.

"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.

"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.

"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."

There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.

A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.

"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.

"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."

Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.

Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.

Other Eyeball, external partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.

"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.

"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.

"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

Sports.title: Advert break during Arsenal Champions League game was unscheduled
Sports.text:
A three-minute advert break during a Women's Champions League game was not scheduled, Disney+ confirmed.

Arsenal and HB Koge were drawing 0-0 in the second half on Tuesday when coverage was interrupted.

It was one of several technical issues during the coverage, which fans said was "gimmicky" and "undermines" women's football. One guest was a dog with 137,000 Instagram followers.

Disney confirmed it was an unintended interruption caused by a technical issue and understood the frustration caused. It was making steps to ensure it did not happen again.

Arsenal won 1-0 in their first game of this season's competition thanks to a stoppage-time Mariona Caldentey penalty.

Disney's coverage also featured a vegetable platter being served and a rotating floor.

Alex Scott hosted the first show of the season, alongside former England forward Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and a dog called Barley Boy.

There was no explanation for his presence on set other than his Instagram following.

It was the second season of the Women's Champions League to be broadcast on Disney+. Matches are produced by ESPN.

New this season is "The Hangout", described by Disney as a live studio show billed as a "new match-day experience for fans, delivering pre-match build-up, half-time analysis and post-match reaction".

In a media release before the first round of fixtures, Disney said: "The Hangout will combine expert analysis with fresh perspectives and fan engagement."

However, the evening was marred by a series of technical issues – from players waiting to be interviewed but unable to hear questions from the studio, to a rotating floor that appeared to have a mind of its own.

There were also camera shots with cushions blocking the view of Scott, and audio synchronisation problems.

Italian reporter Roberto Perrone, in Milan for Inter Milan's match against Swedish side Hacken, also encountered audio problems.

When the sound returned, viewers were shown a non-football-themed quiz, with questions ranging from types of pasta to Italy's biggest city.

One fan wrote on X: "I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women's football broadcasting over analysis and punditry vs content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men's football you can get both - and in different shows.

"In women's football, you get one show, and so they try to do it all."

Another fan wrote: "We want women's football to be taken seriously, yet coverage like this undermines that. Personality and fun have their place, but not at the expense of the football.

"The game doesn't need gimmicks to make it interesting. Give the players, the competition and the football itself the same focus, analysis and respect we expect elsewhere in the sport.

"Women's football is more than capable of being the main event."

Megan Feringa, a journalist for the Athletic, said: "Watching Disney's coverage is like going in and out of a lucid dream.

"Why is there a dog? Why is the couch spinning? Why do the adverts cut right into analysis?"

Flo Lloyd-Hughes, a broadcaster and writer for the Cutback, said: "Why does women's football coverage always have to be so gimmicky? It's the Champions League, not Blue Peter.

"Put some pundits who know about the teams in a studio, make sure the tech works and have a decent bit of time for build-up and analysis to contextualise everything."

Last November concerns were raised over the professionalism and legitimacy of the Women's League Cup quarter-final and semi-final draw, which was conducted by social media influencer GK Barry.

In the same month Sky Sports scrapped its new female-focused TikTok channel, Halo, after it faced a backlash online, with its posts described as "patronising" and "sexist".

Disney+ coverage continues on Wednesday with Chelsea hosting Austria Wien at 20:00 BST.

Sports.title: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks explains the "scary" detail behind emergency appendix surgery
Sports.text:
Will Jacks was supposed to be going to Edinburgh last month to celebrate his mum's 60th birthday.

Instead, what the England all-rounder thought was a "tummy bug" turned out to be appendicitis.

From there, a rushed visit to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh and emergency surgery followed.

"It was just really bad really quickly so we had to go," Jacks, 27, said.

"It was, obviously, completely random and quite scary. I was lucky to be looked after really well by the NHS."

Jacks was given an initial four-week recovery period but ended up returning a few days early to captain the Lions in a warm-up against Sri Lanka on 11 September.

Afterwards he played in all three T20s in England's series sweep against the same opponents, and on Tuesday took career-best 50-over figures of 5-22 in the first one-day international in Chester-le-Street.

"Luckily they were able to do a slight incision and not have to rip me open completely," he said.

Appendix operations are not rare but they do not fit naturally with the twisting and turning of a spin bowler's action, meaning Jacks has been doing extra work behind the scenes to rebuild his core strength.

It makes the 4.3 degrees of turn Jacks found at Chester-le-Street – the most he has produced at home in his ODI career – even more impressive, albeit helped by a slow pitch.

His figures were also the second best by an England spinner in one-day internationals.

"It was more of a confidence thing," he said.

"It helped that we were playing the T20s first and I was bowling a maximum of four overs.

"If I am honest, I only bowled five days before the first game because I was building up my strength and trying to get some fitness back.

"I didn't bowl too much in the T20 series, which probably benefited me. It has been OK."

Jacks' match in the north east also included an important 46 not out with the bat.

Though he was eventually left stranded, he batted responsibly, hitting only one four in his first 43 deliveries, to make sure England's innings was extended from 211-7 in the 39th over to 265 in the penultimate.

"I came in and found it really difficult to start off," he said.

"I just re-evaluated what I thought was a good score and obviously what then happened with wickets falling around me a change of the role, just try and bat out the overs."

For so long "batting out the overs" has not been the England way, but Jacks is a player growing in maturity.

He is also vice-captain to Harry Brook for these Sri Lanka series in the absence of Jacob Bethell and has become an increasingly vocal member of the group.

It was telling that when England's T20 World Cup campaign began earlier this year amid the cloud of Brook's Wellington episode, Jacks was first put up to speak to the media.

"He's just a good leader," Brook said, plainly.

Reliable off the field, Jacks is becoming increasingly so on it.

It is 18 months since he moved from the top of the order to the middle as England's finisher in T20 and 50-over cricket.

After obvious success as England's player of the tournament at the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka, this was another sign of his growing confidence and ability to do what is needed. Finishers rarely arrive in ideal situations, but their impact can often be match-defining.

"I feel very comfortable going out there on the day and any situation can arise which I really enjoy," Jacks said.

"It is not the same every day which you get opening so it keeps that fresh element to the game.

"At the beginning of my career it felt like you are just fighting to play in the next game, which is not the best place to be.

"It is a luxury to know, say when we go to Headingley [for the second ODI], that I will be in the team. You can't take that for granted and appreciate the hard work you have done to get there."

It is also easy to forget Jacks began the year in England's Test side, as their spinning all-rounder during the Ashes - a role now filled by Dan Lawrence.

Jacks, who met new Test coach Stephen Fleming when the New Zealander joined the white-ball squad at Old Trafford last weekend, has signed up for a stint with MI Cape Town in the SA20 this winter.

There would no clash there with Fleming's first tour in charge in South Africa over Christmas, but the later part of the T20 competition overlaps with England's two Tests in Bangladesh, where English spinners will be needed.

"I don't know about what would happen or even if they would want me," he said.

"We will finish the summer before getting into the winter."

For now, Jacks will focus on white-ball trips to Pakistan, Australia and South Africa as England build towards the 50-over World Cup next autumn.

One downside of a Test recall would be losing more time to rearrange that Edinburgh trip.

"It didn't go how we planned but we will have to find time to redo it," Jacks smiled.

Sports.title: Columbus Crew sack Federico Higuain after sexist remark to female referee
Sports.text:
Major League Soccer club Columbus Crew have sacked their reserve team coach after he refused to let go of a female referee's hand and said "don't forget this is a man's game".

Federico Higuain, brother of former Real Madrid striker Gonzalo Higuain, was sent off and given a two-match suspension for the incident during an MLS Next Pro league match.

"We determined it's in the best interest of our club, players and support staff to dismiss Federico Higuain from his responsibilities," Crew general manager Issa Tall said in a statement.

"After conversations this week and further assessing the past month, our club's standards of what's expected from a leader for one of our teams have not been met."

Meanwhile, the Professional Soccer Referees Association (PSRA) criticised the league's response, saying Higuain's two-game ban "falls drastically short".

A statement from the referees' union added: "A male head coach committed two deliberate acts of physical abuse and sexism against a female official - squeezing her hand and refusing to let go after being told to stop three times.

"This physical intimidation was compounded by a demeaning, sexist remark to the official: 'Don't forget, this is a man's game.'

"Women make every level of this game better. They should not have to endure intimidation or degrading comments to prove it.

"Our female officials have proven their excellence on the world stage. They deserve the same respect, dignity, and safe working environment as every other official."

Sports.title: Krystian Bielik: Cardiff City defender charged by FA over Portsmouth incident
Sports.text:
The Football Association has charged Cardiff City defender Krystian Bielik with misconduct over an altercation involving Portsmouth fans, but a police investigation has been concluded and they will take no further action over the incident.

The flashpoint came during Cardiff's 2-0 Championship defeat at Portsmouth on Saturday, 5 September.

The FA stated: "It's alleged that the player [Bielik] acted in an improper manner around the 71st minute of the match."

The Poland international has been given until Friday, 25 September to respond to the FA charge.

Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards, but this has been concluded.

A police statement read: "Following an incident involving a Portsmouth FC supporter and a Cardiff player at Fratton Park on 5 September 2026, we have now concluded our investigation.

"After speaking with the complainant and reviewing all available evidence, the matter has been resolved by way of an out-of-court disposal, agreed by all parties involved. As part of this resolution, an apology has been provided by the player.

"The matter is now considered closed, and no further action will be taken in relation to this incident."

Cardiff City have been asked to comment.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland v Israel: Irish squad will 'come together' to discuss fixtures, says Dara O'Shea
Sports.text:
Dara O'Shea says the Republic of Ireland squad will wait until after Thursday's Kosovo game before discussing how they approach Sunday's contentious fixture against Israel.

The Republic of Ireland face Kosovo in Pristina on Thursday (19:45 BST) before travelling to Debrecen in Hungary for the first of two Israel games in this international window.

There have been increasing calls in Ireland for a boycott of the matches, with a protest held at the Republic of Ireland team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

This followed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, signed by over 160 Irish sportspeople, urging the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) to withdraw from the fixtures because of the situation in Gaza.

O'Shea said it is important for the squad to "speak openly" and "respect each other's views" when they come together to discuss the Israel game on Friday.

"We've got to respect each other's opinions and each other's views and really sit down and take the time, because it deserves the time to talk about," he said.

"It's the main thing and it's something that can't be brushed over. Whatever decision that we go through as players is taken as one and everybody's view is respected as well.

O'Shea, who will captain the Republic of Ireland in the absence of the injured Nathan Collins, added the players have been aware of the "noise" surrounding this window but have tried to avoid it as much as possible.

"The good thing we have as players is when we step into the squad you're in the international bubble straight away," added the Ipswich defender.

"So we've known the noise around the game and there has been, but I think we've all tried to stay off social media as much as possible and stay together."

O'Shea admitted it was a "difficult" and "unusual" situation for the players, who will also face Israel in the Republic of Ireland's 'home' game in the Serbian town of Backa Topola on 4 October.

"We've got a massive game tomorrow that we've been preparing for," he said.

"We've come in on Sunday and that's been our focus straight away was preparing for that game and giving it the amount of effort that it needs.

"Kosovo are a great side and we've been preparing for that."

In February 2024, the Ireland women's basketball team refused to shake hands with Israel and lined up for their anthem beside the team's bench rather than the centre of the court.

Asked if a decision had been made about pre-match formalities, O'Shea said: "We spoke already at the start of the week that we're going to come together on Friday and discuss this as a group.

"Tomorrow we've got a game to focus on, first of all. I don't think we'll be doing our job properly if we didn't put our full focus into that game. Once the game's over and Friday comes, we're all going to come together as one and discuss it openly."

When asked if a boycott of Sunday's Israel game will be discussed among the squad on Friday, O'Shea said: "For us, the decision was made by the FAI, Uefa and the Government. For us as players, that's not our decision.

"We're Irish players and when called upon we come and represent our country and that's important to know too.

"Obviously when we come together, we'll speak openly about what we feel and what we feel is right. And yeah, that'll be given its time on Friday."

Earlier this week, Israel's football governing body accused Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimmson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" regarding comments he made about facing Israel.

Last week, Hallgrimsson said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

While the FAI did not respond publicly, Taoiseach Micheal Martin [Irish prime minister] said Israel FA's comments were "unacceptable" and "should be withdrawn".

Addressing the matter on Wednesday, Hallgrimsson expressed gratitude for the support he has received while admitting "it was not clever" of him to generate headlines in the build-up to the Kosovo match.

"Obviously, we are grateful for all the support that we have," said the Icelander, who has been in charge since 2024.

"Creating and taking over maybe the headlines at the moment, what I said [in the] last press meeting we had is taking the attention away from maybe what's most important," he said.

"We are playing an important game against Kosovo. So that was not the purpose and from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention like this.

"I need to be focused on the game, the players need to be focused on the game. But to answer the question, we're thankful for all the support we get. It's a tricky time for us."

Armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been conducted in self-defence and in accordance with international law.

Sports.title: Cycling Road World Championships 2026: GB medal chance with Pogacar absence
Sports.text:
Great Britain's impressive rider line-up for cycling's Road World Championships means the team have rarely stood a better chance of glory.

For the men, there is also the helpful factor of Slovenian superstar Tadej Pogacar being absent, after he suffered crash injuries during the Vuelta a Espana in August.

But at the same time a new generation of British cycling talent is rising, and GB riders could take the coveted winner's rainbow jersey in the men's and women's road races in Montreal this weekend.

While Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta, the race showcased the continued emergence of 21-year-old British rider Matthew Brennan, who won five stages of the three-week endurance test for Visma Lease a Bike - a record for a Grand Tour debutant.

There are currently 49 British riders competing across the men's and women's world tours - more than ever before - and some of those will compete in this World Championship weekend.

The road race itself is much like a stage of the Tour de France, but in which riders compete in national squads, looking to out-think and out-muscle each other.

A lot of the British potential is thanks to the inspiration of British cycling's golden period, which featured great success from the likes of Team Sky, Mark Cavendish and Lizzie Deignan across the past 15 years.

Deignan won the road race in 2015, while Cavendish triumphed in 2011.

In total, British riders have won the elite road races seven times, including Tom Simpson (1965), Beryl Burton (1960 & 1967), Mandy Jones (1982) and Nicole Cooke (2008).

Amid an unpredictable performance landscape for the women, Britain's best young female riders have a chance to infiltrate the once-dominant Dutch contingent.

Tour de France Femmes winner Demi Vollering remains the sport's best overall, but Briton Zoe Backstedt's brilliant second place in Sunday's Worlds time trial was her first shot at the elite level.

She will be involved in Saturday's women's road race, and Olympic mountain bike gold medallist and Tour de France stage winner Tom Pidcock will race for the men on Sunday.

"You need a lot of faith in your team to be present at the front," Backstedt told BBC Sport. "You need to talk, hear, see and feel each other to know they are there, especially as there's no team radio.

"Obviously it's about knowing the big names to follow. If Demi or Kasia [Niewiadoma] go off the front, you know it's a dangerous move and you need to be there.

"But we've got a super strong team, and if any one of us was with them, we all could stand have a chance."

The women's road race is 180.4km long, which includes eight laps of Montreal, and the men's 273.2km race incorporates 12 circuits.

One key way to win a road race at the Road Worlds is by breaking away from the peloton with a certain distance of the race left to run.

The risk is that one, or a handful, of cyclists find it much harder to win a race by riding into the wind than a peloton of more than 100 riders all taking turns in what can be known as the 'washing machine effect'.

But, if the legs are good and the wind is with them, riders can break away for glory.

"Sometimes you are surprised when you hit the wall, but other times you can push harder and dig deeper," Norway's Sigrid Haugset told the BBC's More Than the Score podcast.

The Uno-X Mobility rider won stage three of this year's Tour de France Femmes after a huge 113km breakaway in which she beat more decorated rivals, such as Belgium's Lotte Kopecky.

"That's the good day - when you feel unstoppable. But I like it when there is plenty of noise [on the team radio from the car]. If it's too little, you get into your head, you feel a bit alone."

Steve Cummings is sporting director at World Tour team Jayco Alula and a former GB rider and breakaway stage winner on both the 2015 and 2016 Tours de France.

Assessing the thrill of a breakaway win, he told More Than the Score: "It's like an underdog victory, and it kind of warms the heart. You have to go all-in. It becomes unpredictable and things can happen tactically and physically - say if a rider pushes too much on a climb.

"That day [in 2015] I did the climb of my life. I was empty for two days after [the 2016 win] and I was in bed for two days after [a Dauphine stage win]. It takes a lot out of you."

Sports.title: Emma Raducanu inspired by Andre Agassi in plotting route back to top of tennis
Sports.text:
As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.

Five years have passed since Raducanu's remarkable US Open triumph, when at the age of 18 she became the first qualifier in the Open era to win a Grand Slam.

American Agassi was a teenage prodigy himself and later claimed the first of his eight major singles titles at Wimbledon in 1992 aged 22.

But between the peak years of his career, he had to overcome a challenging period when he went four years without a major and dropped to 141st in the world rankings.

"I was especially intrigued by the passage where he got out of his slump in the late 1990s by creating his own training regimen and finding his way back to the top," Raducanu told Uniqlo.

"It speaks in depth about his early successes and the lows he reached, perhaps as a result of them.

"A lot of it was so relatable."

Agassi said his hope was for his experiences to help other players going through similar periods in their own careers.

"It's wonderful to hear that anybody can relate," Agassi told BBC Breakfast.

"It was literally the hope that if one person read it and it gave them hope, some tools to understand that they're not alone, they can figure it out and get to a healthier place without having to direct their frustrations at the game of tennis, then it was a success for me.

"So, hearing that 17 years later it can still impact somebody, especially in this game, it does make me feel good."

Raducanu reached a career-high ranking of 10 in July 2022, but the 23-year-old has slipped to 98th in the world.

Her progress continues to be hampered by physical issues, and she most recently missed the US Open as she continues her recovery from a stress fracture in her lower right leg.

A foot injury disrupted her pre-season training before she spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness earlier this year.

But Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career at Queen's Club in June, reaching her biggest final since her triumph in New York five years ago.

Agassi won all four of the sport's Grand Slams and claimed Olympic singles gold at the 1996 Games.

Asked what advice he would give Raducanu, Agassi said: "I would encourage her to focus on being the best of herself on a daily basis, but don't judge that by results or thinking that somehow you have to be 100%.

"You have to learn to be 100% of whatever percent you're at [and] be comfortable in your own identity inside of that - not what people say.

"Back in my day, I could just put down the paper and not read it. Now it seems like it's harder for these youngsters to avoid."

For Agassi, tennis was by no means a childhood passion. His father, keen for his son to become the very best, would introduce him to others as a future number one tennis player.

That additional pressure, Agassi says, led him to play with "fear". It was not until he sank from world number one to 141st that he felt able to reconnect with the sport.

Agassi, who created a foundation providing education for under-served children during that time, said: "I had more success from that point forward than I did playing out of fear.

"The first thing I would advise a parent to think about is that it's not their life, it's their child.

"You raise a child in their way and they'll never depart from it. You just have to find out what their way is."

Agassi will captain Team USA in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London later this week, between 25-27 September.

"Tennis is a hamster wheel of sorts - the fact that these guys make room in their schedule to play this incredible event tells you how great this event is," Agassi added.

"We're obviously playing Team Europe, in Europe, so I don't know where the crowd is going to have their heart.

"But I know one thing - they're going to see some spectacular tennis."

Sports.title: Pocognoli has 'positive nervousness' for Scotland debut
Sports.text:
Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli admits to feeling a "positive nervousness" before his first game in charge of the country, a Nations League tie against Slovenia in Ljubljana on Saturday.

The Belgian was appointed in August, replacing Steve Clarke, whose seven-year tenure ended after Scotland's exit at the group stages of the World Cup.

Pocognoli starts with four Nations League matches across 11 days, with the trip to Slovenia followed by Switzerland at Hampden, a fixture in North Macedonia, then a return meeting with the Slovenes in Glasgow.

"If we talk about nerves, yes, but it's a positive nervousness," he told BBC Sport Scotland. "We have a job with responsibility. It's excitement and I'm just passionate about being on the touchline."

Scotland are currently at a warm weather camp in La Manga, Spain with a much-changed squad.

Pocognoli has picked a 19-year-old in James Wilson, four 20-year-olds - Findlay Curtis, Ben Gannon-Doak, Lennon Miller and Colby Donovan - and another three aged 22 - Kristi Montgomery, Luke Graham and Robbie Ure.

With Blackburn's Montgomery replacing the injured Kenny McLean, there are now eight uncapped players in the squad.

"It's a lot of new faces, so it's a challenge to find the right balance, to keep the cohesion in the team," Pocognoli said.

The manager says he knows his team and his formation for the Slovenia game but is not wedded to any particular system, although playing three at the back has been a staple of his coaching to this point.

"I always think the players select themselves," he added. "We have four games, so we need to plan. We need to have a periodisation [managing training loads, games and recovery] about the tactical aspect and the physical aspect.

"This team can be flexible. We're ready for the four games in terms of what kind of approach we want to give."

Pocognoli revealed he has had a conversation with his predecessor, Clarke - "a nice meeting on the phone," as he put it.

"He was very kind, very... humble. That was very helpful for me. It just was to let me know that he's behind the team. He was very happy [in his time in the job] but he also felt that it was the right time [to leave]. He wished me all the best.

"I will try to be as successful as the previous staff because we want to play in a big tournament. We want to create this moment for the country."

Asked if his brand of football will involve more risk and adventure than Clarke's, he said: "We have to find the right balance because if you play fantastic football and you don't qualify you get some criticism."

Pocognoli's style is all about aggressive pressing and fast tempo. He says that it might take a while for cohesion to be achieved but there are certain things that he wants to see straight away against Slovenia.

"For me, it's about the personality of the players," he added. "I like a unit team who are just fighting for each other.

"It's a basic principle - attack together and squeeze the pitch. When we need to defend, it's just to defend like brothers. When we lose the ball, it's try to regain the ball as quickly as possible.

"From that, there are a lot of other principles, but that's the base. If you cannot get this, you will never have good principles on the pitch."

Given the condensed nature of the games, there is going to be a fair degree of rotation from Slovenia away, to Switzerland at home, to North Macedonia away and Slovenia at home.

"So good so far," Pocognoli said about what he has seen in La Manga. "But we need to get the response through the games. It's up to them to perform well, but it's up to me to make them perform well."

Gaming_Tech.title: Super intelligence: Will Trump’s attempt to rebrand AI work?
Gaming_Tech.text:
US President Donald Trump says the term artificial intelligence (AI) makes the technology "sound fake" and wants it to be called "super intelligence".

"Welcome to the new world of super intelligence - SI," Trump said during a wide-ranging speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

While some people close to the president immediately started to use the term, experts have told the BBC it is unlikely to gain widespread traction in the industry because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

The announcement is Trump's latest rebranding move after he had the names of Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico changed on US maps and federal communications.

"From this point forward, all of United States' documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the more accurate term 'super' as opposed to 'artificial'. So it's 'super intelligence'," Trump said.

In the past week, Trump asked his social media followers to vote on other potential new names for AI including superior intelligence, extreme intelligence and supreme intelligence.

After a series of polls on his Truth Social platform, super intelligence came out as the winner.

The purpose of renaming AI - and whether it will be adopted by the technology industry - is unclear.

AI refers to computer technology that allows machines to do tasks that usually require human thinking.

Meanwhile, super intelligence has a specific meaning within the tech community.

The term is often linked to the author and philosopher Nick Bostrom, who more than a decade ago defined the idea as an "intellect" that is superior to humans in all forms. It is still entirely hypothetical.

The rebranding is "misleading", as super intelligence typically refers to a system that has the ability to improve by itself, said digital ethics lecturer Simon Coghlan from The University of Melbourne.

"I doubt 'SI' will stick, in part because it exaggerates the current capacities of AI," he said.

"A superintelligent system, if it came about, would be regarded by experts as the most consequential technology ever made," Coghlan said.

"Not all AI platforms today exude super intelligence", said computer scientist Kokil Jaidka, adding that the new name "borrows the prestige of a term researchers reserve for a much bigger leap".

National University of Singapore computer science lecturer Ben Leong said: "My guess is that professionals will want to save 'SI' for a higher level of AI, not so much to describe AI today. It doesn't feel like it's at that level yet."

But some in Trump's circle have already started to use the new term.

"The Super Intelligence (SI) President has spoken! The United States is and will remain the global leader in SI," US Chief Technology Officer Ethan Klein wrote on social media.

While Trump's ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz later said: "If you didn't see the president's speech, it's now super intelligence. I think he's absolutely right."

However, when asked for his thoughts on the new name, Canada's minister of AI Evan Solomon said: "Canadians are not enthusiastic, at all, about renaming things," in an apparent reference to Trump renaming Lake Ontario.

Gaming_Tech.title: Data centres: Developers hope fibre optics will cut power use
Gaming_Tech.text:
"I think we're at the end of copper," says Chris Sharp, the chief technology officer at data centre operator Digital Reality.

He's not saying that we are running out of copper, instead Sharp, and many others in the data centre industry, are betting that it will be used less.

Data centres use vast amounts of the metal: around 400 tonnes, external will go into a typical facility of around 100MW (data centre size is measured megawatts, a unit of electrical power).

Most of that copper is used in the electrical infrastructure needed to power the datacentre and for cooling systems. But up to 70 tonnes is used by the computer servers that do the work of processing data in that 100MW facility.

Meanwhile, up to 20 tonnes is used for the network wiring connecting up those computer servers.

It's here, in the spaghetti-like wiring which snakes through a data centre where copper is targeted for replacement.

"The wires between these GPUs, CPUs, and all this compute are what's slowing us down," says Sharp.

Data is shunted around data centres in the form of electrons, which travel efficiently in copper wiring.

Many think there's an even better way of doing that, using light in the form of photons.

Light has been used for decades for long-distance communications over optical fibre - the data for this article probably travelled down a fibre optic cable at some stage.

But researchers and companies want to extend fibre's use to inside the data centre.

It involves intricate engineering, where optical components are connected directly to electrical ones, sometimes on the computer chips themselves.

The technology is called photonics and the big benefit is that light does not have the heating effects of electricity. Less heat means less energy is needed to cool data centre systems.

"You can save so much energy," says Callum Littlejohns, deputy director of silicon photonics foundry Cornerstone Labs.

Photonics are unlikely to make data centres any more popular with the public, but could make them a bit less energy hungry.

Littlejohns also points out that multiple data streams can be transmitted down the same channel to create more capacity.

Peter O'Brien, head of research for photonics packaging and systems integration at Ireland's Tyndall Research Institute, said academics and commercial companies alike have been working with photonics for years, but the technology faced multiple manufacturing challenges.

Now, O'Brien continues, the technology is ready to make the leap from the lab into widespread application.

"What's happening now with optics and photonics is there's kind of a reset," he says.

It helps that AI chip giant Nvidia has thrown its weight behind the technology.

But shifting to photonics is not a straightforward swap, as it brings together different engineering traditions and different supply chains.

"We've really gotten good at bringing the cost down on that electrical side, how to design it, how to manufacture it, how to test it, how to deploy it," says Andrew Wheeler, senior vice president at Hewlett Packard Labs.

But he says, the industry is still working out how to bring the cost down.

Part of the problem is that different elements of the manufacturing process are distributed across the globe. For example final assembly is done in so-called packaging houses, which are clustered in Taiwan.

Engineering challenges remain. Optical networking devices may generate far less heat but other components within a data centre are still making the local environment hot.

And that's a problem for optical components which are very sensitive to heat, explains Wheeler. This raises reliability concerns, unless data centre operators and equipment manufacturers can keep within strict thermal limits.

And while optical networks can carry data at – almost - the speed of light, installing and maintaining them will still proceed at human speed. Network designers, field support engineers, installers, all need to learn new skills around installation and servicing.

For example, says Sharp, with fibre, "You can't take tight turns. There are little nuances on how to structure that."

Ultimately, the benefits of optical networking can only be fully realised when light is used for not just carrying data, but for processing it too, says Ofer Shapiro, CEO of optical company Resolight.ai.

The company is proposing an architecture to replace the traditional electronic network switches that control communications between servers with all optical devices.

He argues that it doesn't make sense to constantly convert data from photons to electrons and back to photons.

Optical interconnects between the computer chips and network elements would mean data would remain in the optical domain, saving even more energy, Shapiro argues.

But that's in the future. More immediately, companies are still working on scaling up photonics manufacturing.

Littlejohns says this ability to reuse knowledge gained through electronics manufacturing will ultimately help lower the cost of photonics.

"We know we can make it huge scale, so that's why it's such an interesting technology, because it can underpin many applications."

Photonics components are generally larger than silicon components, used in computer chips.

Counterintuitively, this means that organizations like Cornerstone can repurpose older silicon manufacturing equipment used for earlier generations of processors.

One of Cornerstone's manufacturing tools comes from a former Intel production line used to make the Pentium 4 chips released back at the turn of the century.

Littlejohns says this ability to reuse knowledge gained through electronics manufacturing will ultimately help lower the cost of photonics.

"We know we can make it at a huge scale, so that's why it's such an interesting technology, because it can underpin many applications."

Gaming_Tech.title: Pornhub age checks investigated by Ofcom
Gaming_Tech.text:
Ofcom has launched an investigation into Pornhub owner, Aylo, over whether the site's new age checks are effectively stopping children from accessing adult content.

The regulator said in May that Pornhub started using a new age verification process for some users, which relied on a third party, Apple.

It said it had concerns that Aylo "may not have conducted sufficient due diligence and testing" before implementing this new process, and so it "may not be highly effective" at preventing children from seeing pornography.

In a lengthy statement given to the BBC, Aylo strongly defended its system for age verification while stressing it would cooperate fully with the investigation.

Under the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA), sites that host pornographic material must use highly effective age assurance to ensure users are over 18, but it leaves it up to the service to decide the method of age-checking it will use.

Ofcom says as part of its investigation it will consider how Aylo implements its age verification processes and whether it conducted the "necessary due diligence" before it was implemented.

It will not investigate how Apple operates its age checks.

George Lusty, Ofcom's Director of Enforcement, said: "Online age checks are a vital protection to prevent children from encountering inappropriate or harmful material, including pornography.

"We expect tech firms to ensure age checks are highly effective before introducing them. Anything less could leave children at risk."

But Aylo argues that, having experimented in multiple markets with multiple age-check methods, Apple's system "provides significantly stronger protection than any other age assurance method currently available in the UK market".

It also notes that Ofcom had previously praised Apple's technology as "a real win for children and families".

Aylo argues a system based on asking individual pornographic sites to check users ages, simply drives users to riskier sites that aren't following Ofcom's rules.

Research by the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, external has previously suggested that non-compliant sites "may also be more likely to host harmful or illegal content, and in some cases, sexual images of children".

But Iain Corby executive director of the Age Verification Providers Association told the BBC that an age-restricted site could not rely on an mobile device based system alone unless it could demonstrate "that children are in fact prevented from accessing its content to the required standard."

He doubted that Apple could show that "each time someone accesses its site, that the person is the same one who originally proved their age to remove the device's filter, or that Apple's filter will always prevent access to all its adult sites."

Under the OSA, Ofcom holds the power to fine non-compliant companies up to £18 million or 10% of their annual global turnover, whichever is greater.

This probe is just the latest clash between the regulator and what is one of the world's most viewed porn sites.

In October 2025 Pornhub said traffic from UK users had plunged by more than 75% following the introduction of more robust age checks by the OSA.

Some have questioned whether people were simply using Virtual Private Networks (VPN) to get around the checks instead.

In January, Pornhub announced it would restrict access to its website in the UK, blaming the tougher checks, with only people who had previously made a Pornhub account able to access its content.

Aylo said that updates to the Act requiring age verification had "not achieved its goal of protecting minors".
